claim: The seventh pandemic of cholera disease began in 1960.
source: The seventh pandemic of the diarrheal cholera disease, which began in 1960, is caused by the Gram-negative bacterium Vibrio cholerae.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by citation in the introduction.

claim: The seventh pandemic of cholera is caused by Vibrio cholerae.
source: The seventh pandemic of the diarrheal cholera disease, which began in 1960, is caused by the Gram-negative bacterium Vibrio cholerae.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is established scientific knowledge.

claim: Vibrio cholerae is a Gram-negative bacterium.
source: The Gram-negative bacterium Vibrio cholerae is the causative agent of the diarrheal cholera disease, which is pandemic since 1960 (Hu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with citation support.

claim: ToxR and ToxS are sensory proteins located at the inner membrane of V. cholerae.
source: Located at the inner membrane, ToxR and ToxS react to environmental stimuli like bile acid, thereby inducing survival strategies for example bile resistance and virulence regulation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract.

claim: ToxR and ToxS react to environmental stimuli like bile acid.
source: Located at the inner membrane, ToxR and ToxS react to environmental stimuli like bile acid, thereby inducing survival strategies for example bile resistance and virulence regulation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The crystal structure of the sensory domains of ToxR and ToxS was determined.
source: The presented crystal structure of the sensory domains of ToxR and ToxS in combination with multiple bile acid interaction studies, reveals that a bile binding pocket of ToxS is only properly folded upon binding to ToxR.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by crystallographic data in the results.

claim: A bile binding pocket of ToxS is only properly folded upon binding to ToxR.
source: The presented crystal structure of the sensory domains of ToxR and ToxS in combination with multiple bile acid interaction studies, reveals that a bile binding pocket of ToxS is only properly folded upon binding to ToxR.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through structural and interaction data.

claim: ToxRS shows structural and functional similarities with VtrAC from V. parahaemolyticus.
source: ToxRSp shows structural and functional similarities with bile sensing complex VtrAC from V. parahaemolyticus (Alnouti, 2009; Li et al., 2016; Tomchick et al., 2016) thus supporting a common superfamily of co-component signal transduction systems whose sensory function is strictly connected to an obligate heterodimer formation (Kinch et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract with citation support and demonstrated through structural comparison.

claim: Cholera causes 21,000–143,000 deaths worldwide per year.
source: Its dangerousness is highlighted by its sudden outbreaks and environmental persistence causing 21 000–143,000 000 deaths worldwide per year (Ali et al., 2015) including long-lasting environmental and economic damage (Kanungo et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: V. cholerae exhibits a life cycle between dormant and virulent state.
source: V. cholerae exhibits a life cycle between dormant and virulent state, enabled by its rapid adaption to changing environments (Almagro-Moreno et al., 2015b; Bari et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: ToxR is a transmembrane transcription factor.
source: ToxR is a transmembrane transcription factor (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) involved in the regulation of numerous genes, not only virulence associated, and can function as an activator, co-activator and repressor (Bina et al., 2003; Champion et al., 1997; Lee et al., 2000; Morgan et al., 2011; Skorupski and Taylor, 1997; Wang et al., 2002; Welch and Bartlett, 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations.

claim: ToxR periplasmic domain can bind bile acids.
source: ToxR periplasmic domain is proposed to act as environmental sensor, being able to bind bile acids (Midgett et al., 2017; Midgett et al., 2020) and consequently activate transcription with its cytoplasmic DNA binding domain (Gubensäk et al., 2021a; Morgan et al., 2011; Morgan et al., 2019; Pfau and Taylor, 1996; Withey and DiRita, 2006), thus inducing a switch of outer membrane proteins from OmpT to OmpU (Simonet et al., 2003; Wibbenmeyer et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Bile-induced ToxR activation induces a switch of outer membrane proteins from OmpT to OmpU.
source: ToxR periplasmic domain is proposed to act as environmental sensor, being able to bind bile acids (Midgett et al., 2017; Midgett et al., 2020) and consequently activate transcription with its cytoplasmic DNA binding domain (Gubensäk et al., 2021a; Morgan et al., 2011; Morgan et al., 2019; Pfau and Taylor, 1996; Withey and DiRita, 2006), thus inducing a switch of outer membrane proteins from OmpT to OmpU (Simonet et al., 2003; Wibbenmeyer et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: OmpU is more efficient in excluding bile salts due to its negatively charged pore.
source: Since OmpU is more efficient in excluding bile salts due to its negatively charged pore (Duret and Delcour, 2006; Simonet et al., 2003), bile-induced ToxR activation enables V. cholerae survival in the human gut (Wibbenmeyer et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: ToxS periplasmic domain interacts with ToxR periplasmic domain forming a stable heterodimer.
source: The periplasmic domain of ToxS (ToxSp) interacts with the periplasmic domain of ToxR (ToxRp) forming a stable heterodimer (ToxRSp; Gubensäk et al., 2021b) thereby protecting ToxR from periplasmic proteolysis and enhancing its activity (Almagro-Moreno et al., 2015a; Almagro-Moreno et al., 2015c; Gubensäk et al., 2021b; Lembke et al., 2018; Pennetzdorfer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: ToxS protects ToxR from periplasmic proteolysis.
source: The periplasmic domain of ToxS (ToxSp) interacts with the periplasmic domain of ToxR (ToxRp) forming a stable heterodimer (ToxRSp; Gubensäk et al., 2021b) thereby protecting ToxR from periplasmic proteolysis and enhancing its activity (Almagro-Moreno et al., 2015a; Almagro-Moreno et al., 2015c; Gubensäk et al., 2021b; Lembke et al., 2018; Pennetzdorfer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: ToxR binds DNA as a homodimer at 'tox-boxes' which represent direct repeat DNA motifs.
source: The exact mechanism of ToxR functionality is not clear yet, it was proposed that ToxR binds DNA as a homodimer at the so called 'tox-boxes' which represent direct repeat DNA motifs (Crawford et al., 1998; Goss et al., 2013; Krukonis and DiRita, 2003; Ottemann and Mekalanos, 1996; Pfau and Taylor, 1996; Withey and DiRita, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: ToxR uses a topological DNA recognition mechanism by recognizing DNA structural elements rather than base sequences.
source: Recently, it was shown that ToxR uses a topological DNA recognition mechanism by recognizing DNA structural elements rather than base sequences (Canals et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: The crystal structure of ToxRSp was determined by molecular replacement using an AlphaFold model as template.
source: ToxRSp crystal structure was determined by molecular replacement using an AlphaFold (Evans et al., 2021; Jumper et al., 2021) model as template.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1 caption.

claim: ToxRp β strand 5 completes main chain hydrogen bond network of ToxSp β-barrel formation by interaction with ToxSp β1.
source: ToxRp ß strand 5 completes main chain hydrogen bond network of ToxSp ß-barrel formation, by interaction with ToxSp ß1.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1 caption and shown in the figure.

claim: ToxRp β5 and α2 are formed upon ToxSp interaction.
source: ToxRp ß5 and α2 are formed upon ToxSp interaction.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1 caption and shown in the figure.

claim: ToxSp L33S mutant results in a loss of ToxSp protective function against ToxRp proteolysis.
source: According to previous studies ToxSp L33S mutant results in a loss of ToxSp protective function against ToxRp proteolysis (Pfau and Taylor, 1998).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 caption with citation.

claim: ToxSp L33 has a central function in stabilizing the N-terminal membrane oriented core.
source: ToxRSp crystal structure reveals a central function of ToxSp L33 in stabilizing the N-terminal membrane oriented core visible in the zoomed region.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 caption and shown in the figure.

claim: VtrAC and ToxRSp reveal a similar fold with RMSD of 3.8 Å.
source: VtrAC (gold; pdb: 5KEV) and ToxRSp (dark blue; pdb: 8ALO) reveal a similar fold (RMSD: 3.8 Å).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 caption and shown in the figure.

claim: VtrC and ToxSp form a β-barrel fold which is stabilized by β-strand 5 from VtrA and ToxRp.
source: VtrC and ToxSp form a ß-barrel fold, which is stabilized by ß-strand 5 from VtrA and ToxRp, resulting in an obligate heterodimer formation including a binding pocket in the barrel cavity.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 caption and shown in the figure.

claim: The ToxRSp complex forms spontaneously upon addition of both proteins.
source: The complex forms spontaneously upon addition of both proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: ToxRp in the complex has an αβ fold formed by an α-helix flanked by an anti-parallel hairpin and a three-stranded anti-parallel β-sheet, followed by a C-terminal helix.
source: ToxRp in the complex has an αß fold which is formed by an α-helix flanked by an anti-parallel hairpin and a three-stranded anti-parallel ß-sheet, followed by a C-terminal helix (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1.

claim: ToxRp C-terminal Cys293 is involved in a solution-oriented disulphide bond with Cys236.
source: The C-terminal Cys293ToxRp is involved in a solution-oriented disulphide bond with Cys236ToxRp of the N-terminal helix (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3.

claim: ToxSp forms a lipocalin-like fold consisting of an eight-stranded β-barrel.
source: ToxSp forms a lipocalin-like fold consisting of an eight-stranded ß-barrel stabilized by intermolecular H-bond network and flanked by two α-helices located at the openings of the barrel (Figure 2, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: ToxRp β5 is positioned into the gap between ToxSp β1 and β8 and forms main chain H-bonds with ToxSp β1 residues.
source: ToxRp ß5 is positioned into this gap and forms main chain H-bonds with remaining ToxSp ß1 residues.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: ToxRp Arg281 forms an intermolecular salt bridge with ToxSp Asp142.
source: The residue Arg281 located in ToxRp ß5 forms an intermolecular salt bridge with Asp142 of ToxSp α2, which restricts the opening of the barrel (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: SAXS experiments indicate a dimer formation of ToxSp in the absence of ToxRp.
source: Small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) experiments indicate a dimer formation of ToxSp in the absence of ToxRp (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1c) supporting the recently proposed HDOCK ToxS-ToxS dimer (Canals et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to SAXS data.

claim: Aggregation of ToxSp in solution occurs rapidly suggesting an unstable dimer formation.
source: Nevertheless, aggregation of ToxSp in solution occurs rapidly suggesting an unstable dimer formation (Gubensäk et al., 2021b; Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation and data reference.

claim: Unbound ToxRp has a long intrinsically disordered C-terminus in solution.
source: Unbound ToxRp has a long intrinsically disordered C-terminus in solution, containing the second cysteine Cys293ToxRp forming a disulphide bond with Cys236 ToxRp located in the middle of helix 1 (Gubensäk et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation support.

claim: When bound to ToxSp, the unstructured region of the C-terminus of ToxRp performs a disorder to order transition by forming two additional structural elements: short α helix 2 and β strand 5.
source: When bound to ToxSp, the unstructured region of the C-terminus of ToxRp performs a disorder to order transition, by forming two additional structural elements: short α helix 2 and ß strand 5 (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3.

claim: ToxRSp bile interaction was confirmed using NMR, MMS, size exclusion chromatography, and SAXS.
source: ToxRSp bile interaction was tested using NMR (Becker et al., 2018) (saturation transfer difference STD Figure 6—figure supplement 3, Figure 6—figure supplement 4), chemical shift perturbation CSP (Figure 7, Figure 6—figure supplement 5) and diffusion ordered spectroscopy DOSY (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 6), as well microfluidic modulation spectroscopy MMS (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), size exclusion chromatography (Figure 6C) and SAXS (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with references to multiple experimental techniques.

claim: All interaction experiments confirm an interaction of the ToxRSp complex with bile.
source: All mentioned experiments confirm an interaction of the ToxRSp complex with bile.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section summarizing experimental findings.

claim: MMS experiments show conformational changes of ToxRSp upon binding of bile.
source: MMS experiments of ToxRSp with different S-CH concentrations show conformational changes upon binding of bile to ToxRSp.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 4 caption and shown in the figure.

claim: The lipocalin-like fold of ToxSp forms a hydrophobic cavity.
source: The lipocalin-like fold of ToxSp forms a hydrophobic cavity (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), similar to the bile binding pocket of VtrC in complex with VtrA from V. parahaemolyticus (Tomchick et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Upon binding of bile acid, mainly loop regions of ToxRSp undergo major conformational changes.
source: Upon binding of bile acid mainly loop regions undergo major conformational changes (Figure 4, Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: ToxSp β1/β2 loop and ToxRp α1/β2 loop experience strongest rearrangements upon bile binding.
source: Comparison of ToxRSp apo and bile-bound state reveals that ToxSp β1/β2 loop and ToxRp α1/β2 loop experience strongest rearrangements, whereas loop β3/β4ToxSp, α1ToxSp, α2ToxSp and loop β3/β4ToxRp reveal only minor structural changes (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The nature of the interactions of bile acid with the ToxRSp complex are mostly hydrophobic.
source: The nature of the interactions of bile acid with the protein complex are mostly hydrophobic.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on MD simulation analysis.

claim: Cholate interacts with residues Ser44ToxSp, Ile135ToxSp, Leu138ToxSp, Phe139ToxSp, Val283ToxRp, and Arg281ToxRp.
source: Additionally, cholate interacts with residues Ser44ToxSp, Ile135ToxSp, Leu138ToxSp, Phe139ToxSp, Val283ToxRp, and Arg281ToxRp (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Both ToxRp and ToxSp contribute to the bile acid interaction, although ToxSp residues form a major part of the interface.
source: Both proteins contribute to the bile acid interaction, although ToxSp residues are forming a major part of the interface.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis.

claim: SEC-SAXS experiments indicate an increase of molecular weight, radius of gyration and effective maximum particle dimension of ToxRSp upon addition of equimolar amounts of bile acid.
source: SEC-SAXS experiments indicate an increase of molecular weight, radius of gyration and effective maximum particle dimension of ToxRSp upon addition of equimolar amounts of bile acid (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: NMR DOSY experiments show a decrease of the diffusion coefficient of ToxRSp upon bile acid binding, which is linked to an increase of size and weight.
source: NMR DOSY experiments of ToxRSp bound to bile acid clearly show a decrease of the diffusion coefficient, which is linked to an increase of size and weight (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: MMS experiments indicate that no severe structural rearrangements like aggregation events occur upon bile acid binding to ToxRSp.
source: Via MMS experiments conformational changes could be detected upon bile acid binding but clearly indicate that no severe structural rearrangements for example aggregation events occur (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: MD simulations identified four solvent exposed regions of ToxRSp that show transient binding of cholate molecules.
source: Four solvent exposed regions of the protein, which show a transient binding of cholate molecules could be identified (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Interaction experiments do not indicate a bile induced dimerization or oligomerization event of ToxRSp.
source: Interaction experiments therefore do not implement a bile induced dimerization or oligomerization event.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of experimental data.

claim: The dissociation constant of ToxRp binding to bile acid is 2.6±1.42 mM.
source: The determined dissociation constant of 2.6±1.42 mM (Figure 8, Supplementary file 1d) exhibits a weak binding affinity of ToxRp to bile but physiologically still relevant (Qin and Gronenborn, 2014; Sukenik et al., 2017) since bile acid concentrations in the small intestine vary between 2 and 10 mM (Hamilton et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8.

claim: Bile acid concentrations in the small intestine vary between 2 and 10 mM.
source: The determined dissociation constant of 2.6±1.42 mM (Figure 8, Supplementary file 1d) exhibits a weak binding affinity of ToxRp to bile but physiologically still relevant (Qin and Gronenborn, 2014; Sukenik et al., 2017) since bile acid concentrations in the small intestine vary between 2 and 10 mM (Hamilton et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation support.

claim: Interaction experiments with ToxSp alone and S-CH did not reveal any binding event.
source: Interaction experiments with ToxSp alone and S-CH did not reveal any binding event (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: Without stabilization by ToxRp, the bile binding pocket of ToxSp is not properly formed.
source: Due to ToxSp structural instability (Gubensäk et al., 2021b) we propose that without stabilization of ToxRp, the binding pocket is not properly formed and therefore binding to bile cannot occur.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural instability of ToxSp and lack of bile binding in the absence of ToxRp.

claim: Bile-induced ToxRS activation leads to a change of outer membrane protein production from OmpT to OmpU to achieve bile resistance.
source: In order to achieve bile resistance, ToxRS bile induced activation leads to a change of outer membrane protein production from OmpT to OmpU (Morgan et al., 2011; Provenzano and Klose, 2000; Simonet et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: Correct heterodimer assembly of ToxRSp is critical for efficient bile sensing functionality.
source: Interaction experiments show that correct heterodimer assembly of ToxRSp is critical for efficient bile sensing functionality.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on experimental findings.

claim: Structural changes of the periplasmic domains of ToxRS upon bile recognition are passed on through the ToxR transmembrane domain to its cytoplasmic effector domain.
source: Thus, we suggest that the observed structural changes of the periplasmic domains of ToxRS upon bile recognition are passed on through the ToxR transmembrane domain to its cytoplasmic effector domain, thereby enhancing ToxR binding to recognition sequences and subsequently induction of transcription (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on observed structural changes and known signal transduction mechanisms.

claim: Higher additions of bile acid induce additional structural changes of ToxRSp as shown by MMS experiments.
source: Higher additions of bile acid induce additional structural changes of ToxRSp as shown by MMS experiments (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Postprandial bile acid concentrations are around 10 mM in the initial region of the small intestine, whereas the distal part contains 2 mM bile acids.
source: Bile acid concentrations also vary within the SI: postprandial bile acid concentrations are around 10 mM in the initial region of the SI, whereas the distal part contains 2 mM bile acids. (Hamilton et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: ToxRSp interaction involves a binding site of ToxRSp barrel hosting one bile molecule and multiple surface exposed binding regions offering attachment sites for bile acid molecules.
source: ToxRSp interaction involves a binding site of ToxRSp barrel hosting one bile molecule and multiple surface exposed binding regions offering attachment sites for bile acid molecules.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on experimental and computational findings.

claim: The presented experiments do not indicate a bile-induced dimer- or oligomerization of the ToxRS complex.
source: The presented experiments do not indicate a bile-induced dimer- or oligomerization of the ToxRS complex, which is currently proposed as the active conformation of ToxR.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on experimental findings.

claim: ToxRS and VtrAC are both Vibrio protein complexes that induce virulence by sensing bile via direct interaction.
source: ToxRS and VtrAC (Tomchick et al., 2016) are both Vibrio protein complexes fulfilling an essential function since they induce virulence by sensing bile via direct interaction (Bina et al., 2021; Hay et al., 2017; Hung and Mekalanos, 2005; Tomchick et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: ToxRSp and VtrAC share the β-barrel lipocalin-like formation completed by a β strand, together forming a bile binding pocket.
source: Structurally, the protein complexes share the ß-barrel lipocalin-like formation of ToxSp/VtrC completed by a ß strand of ToxRp/VtrA, together forming a bile binding pocket (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: VtrC is not stable without its interaction partner and tends to aggregate easily, similar to ToxSp.
source: Similar to ToxSp, VtrC is not stable without its interaction partner and tends to aggregate easily (Tomchick et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: In VtrAC, bile binding strictly involves only VtrC, whereas in ToxRSp both proteins contribute to direct interaction with bile.
source: Another difference between the complexes is that VtrA does not contain cysteine residues like ToxRp. The disulphide linkage represents another option for regulation in V. cholerae. Also, bile interaction occurs in a different manner. Whereas in ToxRSp both proteins contribute to the direct interaction with bile, in VtrAC bile binding strictly involves only VtrC (Li et al., 2016; Tomchick et al., 2016; Zou et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: V. cholerae ToxRS was proposed as a distant homolog to VtrAC, forming together a superfamily of co-component signalling systems.
source: Recently, V. cholerae ToxRS was proposed as a distant homolog to VtrAC, forming together a superfamily of co-component signalling systems which are not linked to sequence homology (Kinch et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: The formation of an obligate heterodimer to fold the barrel including the binding pocket is unique for ToxRSp and VtrAC.
source: Although the eight-stranded ß-barrel fold of ToxS and VtrC shows similarities with the calycin superfamily (including fatty acid binding proteins FABP and lipocalins; Supplementary file 1f; Kinch et al., 2022; Tomchick et al., 2016), the formation of an obligate heterodimer to fold the barrel including the binding pocket is unique for ToxRSp and VtrAC (Tomchick et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: VtrAC and ToxRSp remain the only experimentally solved structures of the VtrAC-like superfamily.
source: So far VtrAC and ToxRSp remain the only experimentally solved structures of this relatively new defined superfamily.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The predicted protein structures of ToxRSp proteins from different Vibrio strains share the distinctive ToxRSp fold consisting of a β-barrel ToxSp and an αβ folded ToxRp.
source: The predicted protein structures of ToxRSp proteins from different Vibrio strains (Supplementary file 1e) share the distinctive ToxRSp fold consisting of a ß-barrel ToxSp and an αß folded ToxRp (Figure 10, Fig. Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 10.

claim: The barrel shaped lipocalin-like structure of ToxSp is consistent across different Vibrio strains, whereas ToxRp structure varies among the strains.
source: Although ToxRp structure varies among the strains, the barrel shaped lipocalin-like structure of ToxSp is consistent, clearly visible in the alignment of all structures (Figure 11, Figure 11—figure supplement 1, Figure 11—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 11.

claim: Most conserved residues of ToxSp are located at the openings of the barrel and β strands 8, 7 and 6 which are involved in ToxRp interaction.
source: Most of the conserved residues of ToxSp are located at the openings of the barrel as well as ß strands 8, 7 and 6 which are involved in ToxRp interaction (Figure 11).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 11.

claim: The aspartate residue involved in the intermolecular salt bridge with ToxRp is conserved in ToxSp across Vibrio species.
source: The aspartate residue which is involved in the intermolecular salt bridge with ToxRp is also one of the conserved residues of ToxSp (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: ToxRp sequence is only conserved between human colonizing Vibrio strains.
source: Compared to ToxSp, ToxRp sequence seems to be only conserved between human colonizing strains (Figure 11—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 2.

claim: ToxRp residues involved in the binding to S-CH are conserved.
source: ToxRp residues involved in the binding to S-CH are also conserved (Val283ToxRp, Arg281ToxRp).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on sequence analysis.

claim: The crystal structure of ToxRSp was deposited at the PDB with accession code 8ALO.
source: The structure was deposited at the PDB with the DOI: https://doi.org/10.2210/pdb8ALO/pdb and the PDB accession code 8ALO.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Crystals of ToxRSp diffracted up to 3 Å and belong to the space group P65.
source: Crystals diffracted up to 3 Å and belong to the space group P65 with cell constants of 72.5 Å, 72.5 Å, 79.4 Å and 90°, 90° and 120°.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The ToxRSp structure was solved with molecular replacement using Phaser.
source: The structure was solved with molecular replacement using Phaser (2.8.3) (McCoy et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: A partial ab initio model of the assembled complex of ToxSp and ToxRp predicted by AlphaFold-Multimer was used as a template for molecular replacement.
source: A partial ab initio model of the assembled complex of ToxSp and ToxRp predicted by AlphaFold-Multimer (Evans et al., 2021) was used as a template.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.
